entry: Czech-American former professional [[Tennis|tennis]] player. She was world No. 1 in women's singles for 332 weeks and in women's doubles for a record 237 weeks. Navratilova won 59 major titles, an Open Era record, including nine Wimbledon singles titles and a record six consecutive singles majors across 1983 and 1984. She was one of three players, with [[Margaret Court]] and Doris Hart, to complete a career [[Grand Slam (tennis)|Grand Slam]] in singles, doubles and mixed doubles. Originally from [[Czechoslovakia]], she asked the United States for political asylum in 1975 and became a U.S. citizen in 1981. She has been openly gay since 1981 and has been an activist for gay rights.

Island and overseas region of [[France]] in the [[Lesser Antilles]], eastern Caribbean Sea (pop., 2024: 349,925). It covers 1,128 sq km (436 sq mi). Martinique is an outermost region of the European Union but is not part of the [[Schengen Area]] or the EU customs union, and it uses the [[Euro|euro]]. French is the sole official language. Spain ceded the island to France in 1635, after 133 years of Spanish rule; French settlers under Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc landed that year and claimed it for [[Louis XIII]]. Plantation agriculture relied on enslaved Africans until emancipation in 1848. The 1902 eruption of [[Mount Pelée]] destroyed Saint-Pierre and killed approximately 30,000 people. Bananas, rum and tourism are major economic activities.

American media franchise and shared universe of superhero films produced by Marvel Studios, based on characters from [[Marvel Comics]]. Its first film, *Iron Man* (2008), began Phase One, and the first three phases form the Infinity Saga. The Walt Disney Company owns the franchise, which includes films and television series, including those on Disney+. It is one of the highest-grossing media franchises of all time. Many films of the later Multiverse Saga performed below expectations, a shortfall the studio attributed to the amount of content it produced after *Avengers: Endgame* (2019).

American [[Comic book|comic book]] publisher, a property of The Walt Disney Company since 2009. Founded in 1939 by Martin Goodman as Timely Comics, the company was known as Atlas Comics by 1951. The Marvel era began in 1961 with *The Fantastic Four*, created by [[Stan Lee]], [[Jack Kirby]] and Steve Ditko. Its characters include [[Spider-Man]], [[Captain America]], [[Iron Man]], the Hulk, the [[X-Men]] and Wolverine. Most of its characters share a single fictional reality known as the Marvel Universe, with many major characters based in New York City.

American [[Rhythm and blues|R&B]] and [[Soul music|soul]] singer, songwriter and record producer. He began in Harvey Fuqua's group, Harvey and the Moonglows, and started a solo career in the early 1960s, signing with Motown's Tamla label. His hits included "How Sweet It Is (to Be Loved by You)" and "I Heard It Through the Grapevine". After the album *What's Going On* (1971), he was among the first Motown artists to produce his own albums, including *Let's Get It On*. After moving to [[Columbia Records]] in 1982, he released *Midnight Love* and its single "Sexual Healing", his most successful release, which brought him an American Music Award and two [[Grammy Awards]]. Gaye was shot and killed by his father on the eve of his 45th birthday; the father later pleaded no contest to voluntary manslaughter. Gaye was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

American comedy troupe of five brothers, noted for performances in [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]], on Broadway and in film. Groucho, Harpo and Chico, with Gummo and Zeppo for part of the time, were guided by their mother, Minnie Marx. After vaudeville circuits banned them in 1923 following a dispute with E. F. Albee, they found success on Broadway with *I'll Say She Is* and *Animal Crackers*. They made thirteen feature films, beginning with a 1929 adaptation of *The Cocoanuts* for [[Paramount Pictures]]. Later, at [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]], they worked with producer [[Irving Thalberg]], and *A Night at the Opera* (1935) was their favorite. The American Film Institute named five of their films among the top 100 comedies. Groucho later hosted the quiz show *You Bet Your Life*.

Political philosophy and method of socioeconomic analysis based on historical materialism, developed by [[Karl Marx]] and [[Friedrich Engels]] in the 19th century. Marxism treats class struggle as the central driving force of historical change and holds that a society's economic mode of production shapes its social, political and intellectual life. It argues that the [[Bourgeoisie|bourgeoisie]], who own the means of production, exploit the [[Working class|working class]], and that this leads to alienation, periodic economic crises and class conflict. Marx theorized that workers' revolutions would overthrow [[Capitalism|capitalism]] and establish [[Socialism|socialism]], a transition toward a classless and stateless society. The most prominent 20th-century form was [[Marxism–Leninism]], the official ideology of the Soviet Union. Other traditions, including Western Marxism and Marxist feminism, have often been critical of state socialism. Marxist concepts such as alienation and class struggle have become integral to the social sciences and humanities.

Communist ideology that was the predominant ideology of most communist governments in the 20th century. It was developed in the Soviet Union by [[Joseph Stalin]], drawing on Bolshevism, Leninism and Classical Marxism, and served as the state ideology of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc. It holds that a two-stage communist revolution is needed to replace capitalism, led by a vanguard party that establishes a one-party state. It remains the official ideology of the ruling parties of [[China]], [[Cuba]], [[Laos]] and [[Vietnam]]. After [[Vladimir Lenin|Lenin]]'s death, Stalin and his supporters gained control of the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union]] and adopted the doctrine of socialism in one country. Some historians attribute the repression of communist states to the ideology, while others focus on the actions of leaders such as Stalin and [[Mao Zedong]]. Some academics describe Marxism–Leninism in practice as a form of state capitalism.

American religious leader and author who founded the [[Christian Science]] movement. In 1879 she founded The Church of Christ, Scientist, the Mother Church of the movement, and in 1908 she founded *The Christian Science Monitor*. Her central book, *Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures*, was first published in 1875 and republished many times. Eddy taught that physical ailments stem from erroneous beliefs and can be overcome through spiritual understanding, and she promoted [[Prayer|prayer]] as an alternative to medicine and surgery. Christian Scientists honor her as the "Discoverer and Founder of Christian Science". Critics, including former members, argue that her methods were harmful and ineffective and point to preventable deaths, particularly among children.

Queen of England and Ireland (r. 1553–58) and queen consort of Spain from 1556 as the wife of King Philip II. The only surviving child of [[Henry VIII]] and his first wife, [[Catherine of Aragon]], Mary was declared illegitimate after her parents' marriage was annulled in 1533, but she was restored to the succession. She was the first queen regnant of England, excluding the disputed reigns of Lady Jane Grey and Empress Matilda. Mary attempted to reverse the English Reformation, but Parliament largely thwarted her effort to restore Church property. During her reign more than 280 religious dissenters were burned at the stake, earning her the nickname "Bloody Mary". After her death, her Catholic restoration was reversed by her half-sister and successor, [[Elizabeth I]].

American singer, songwriter and actress, known as the Queen of Hip-Hop Soul. Blige signed to Uptown Records in 1988, and her debut album, *What's the 411?* (1992), is credited with introducing the mix of R&B and hip hop into mainstream pop. She has won nine [[Grammy Awards]], and her single "Family Affair" reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100. Blige received two Academy Award nominations for *Mudbound* (2017), for her supporting role and for the song "Mighty River". She was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2024.

Follower of [[Jesus]] and witness to his crucifixion and resurrection, according to the four canonical gospels. Scholars accept her as a historical figure, but little is known of her life. Her epithet probably refers to Magdala, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee. Luke's gospel says Jesus exorcised seven demons from her, and she supported his ministry financially. A 591 sermon by [[Pope Gregory I]] led to a Western tradition of identifying her as a repentant prostitute, which the Bible does not support. The [[Eastern Orthodox Church]] honors her as a myrrhbearer and "Equal to the Apostles", while Catholic tradition calls her the "Apostle to the Apostles". Relics attributed to her are preserved in France and on [[Mount Athos]].

Canadian-born American film actress and producer, a leading star of the [[Silent film|silent era]]. Born Gladys Louise Smith in [[Toronto]], she began her film career in 1909 and became Hollywood's first millionaire by 1916. At the height of her career she had complete creative control of her films, and she was known as the "Queen of the Movies" and "America's Sweetheart". In 1919 she co-founded United Artists with [[Charlie Chaplin]], [[D. W. Griffith]] and Douglas Fairbanks. She was one of the 36 founders of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 1927. She received the second Academy Award for Best Actress, for *Coquette* (1929), her first sound film, and an honorary Academy Award in 1976.

1964 American musical comedy film directed by Robert Stevenson and produced by [[Walt Disney]]. Based on P. L. Travers's book series, it combines live action with animation and stars Julie Andrews, in her feature film debut, as a nanny who improves a dysfunctional London family. *Mary Poppins* was released on August 27, 1964, and was the highest-grossing film of that year in the United States. It received thirteen [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations, a record for a Disney film, and won five, including Best Actress for Andrews.

Queen of Scotland (r. 1542–67) and queen consort of France (1559–60). Born six days before her father's death, she succeeded to the Scottish throne as an infant. Sent to France as a child, she married the French dauphin Francis in 1558. She returned to Scotland in 1561 to rule a realm divided by religion, facing criticism from [[John Knox]]. In 1565 she married her cousin Lord Darnley, and the marriage soured. After Darnley was murdered in 1567, she married James Hepburn, 4th Earl of Bothwell, who was generally believed to have orchestrated the murder. She was forced to abdicate in favor of her infant son, James VI. Fleeing to England, she was held there for many years by [[Elizabeth I]], and she was beheaded after being found guilty of plotting against Elizabeth. Her life made her a romanticized figure in popular culture.

English novelist and author of the Gothic novel *Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus* (1818), an early work of science fiction. She was the daughter of [[Mary Wollstonecraft]] and the philosopher William Godwin. In 1814 she began a relationship with the poet [[Percy Bysshe Shelley]], who was already married, and the couple married in late 1816 after the suicide of his first wife. During a summer near [[Geneva]] with [[Lord Byron]] in 1816, she conceived the idea for *Frankenstein*. Her husband drowned in 1822, after which she raised their son and worked as a professional author. Her other novels include *Valperga* (1823), *The Last Man* (1826) and *Lodore* (1835). She also edited and promoted her husband's works, and recent scholarship has stressed her political radicalism.

American actress, comedian, singer and songwriter. Discovered by [[Jack Nicholson]] at the [[Paramount Pictures]] office in New York, she made her film debut in his Western comedy *Goin' South* (1978). She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress and the Golden Globe Award for the same role in *Melvin and Howard* (1980). Her other films include *Back to the Future Part III* (1990), *Philadelphia* (1993) and *Book Club* (2018). She has also written songs for films, and her song "Glasgow (No Place Like Home)" from *Wild Rose* (2018) won the Critics' Choice Movie Award for Best Song.

American actress and television producer, known for *The Dick Van Dyke Show* and *The Mary Tyler Moore Show*. She played Laura Petrie on the first series from 1961 to 1966, and Mary Richards on her own series from 1970 to 1977, which she co-produced. Her work won seven Primetime Emmy Awards, three Golden Globe Awards and two Tony Awards. She was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Ordinary People* (1980). Moore was diagnosed with type 1 [[Diabetes|diabetes]] at age 33 and became a significant contributor to diabetes research. She also advocated for [[Animal rights|animal rights]] and vegetarianism.

First-century Jewish woman of [[Nazareth]], mother of [[Jesus]] and a central figure of Christianity. According to the gospels of Matthew and Luke, she conceived Jesus through the Holy Spirit while a virgin, and she gave birth to him in [[Bethlehem]]. She was present at his crucifixion and with the apostles after his ascension. The Catholic Church and Eastern Orthodox churches regard her as the Mother of God, and the Catholic Church teaches her Immaculate Conception and bodily Assumption into heaven. Many Protestants hold more limited views of her role. In [[Islam]] she has the highest position of any woman and is named in the [[Quran]], which has a chapter named after her.

U.S. state on the Mid-Atlantic coast (pop., 2020: 6,177,224). Its capital is Annapolis and its largest city is Baltimore. One of the original [[Thirteen Colonies]], Maryland was chartered in 1632 to the Calvert family, Barons Baltimore, and settled in 1634 as a religious haven for persecuted Catholics. Its early economy relied on tobacco plantations and enslaved labor. Maryland remained in the Union during the [[American Civil War]]. Its economy now spans government, information technology, biotechnology and health care, and in 2015 it had the highest median household income of any state.

Florentine painter regarded as the first great Italian painter of the Quattrocento. He joined the Florentine painters' guild in 1422 and was one of the first artists to use linear [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]] and vanishing points. He moved away from the elaborate ornamentation of the International Gothic style toward a more naturalistic mode, using perspective and chiaroscuro for greater realism. His works include the San Giovenale Triptych and the fresco cycle in the Brancacci Chapel, executed with Masolino in [[Florence]]. Despite a brief career, he influenced many artists, and [[Michelangelo]] studied his frescoes. On hearing of his death, [[Filippo Brunelleschi]] called it a great loss.

Human, animal or object thought to bring luck, or a figure representing a group with a common public identity, such as a school, sports team or brand. Sports teams often choose mascots related to their nicknames, such as the University of Alabama's elephant, Big Al, whose teams are the Crimson Tide. Mascots may be logos, live animals or costumed characters, and since the mid-20th century costumed characters have been popular. Stylistic changes in puppetry, including the work of [[Jim Henson]], were adapted to sports mascots. Costumed mascots are used as goodwill ambassadors for teams, companies and organizations. The word comes from the French *mascotte*, meaning lucky charm. Critics argue that mascots based on ethnic stereotypes, particularly Native American motifs, harm targeted groups, and some professional teams have rebranded.

City in northeastern [[Iran]], about 740 kilometres east of [[Tehran]] and capital of Razavi Khorasan province (pop., 2016: about 3,400,000). It is Iran's second-most-populous city. It takes its name, meaning "place of martyrdom", from the Imam Reza shrine, where the eighth Shia Imam is buried. The Abbasid caliph [[Harun al-Rashid]] is also buried in the shrine, which is the most visited pilgrimage site in Islam, with nearly 30 million visitors each year. Mashhad is associated with [[Ferdowsi]], author of the *Shahnameh*, who was born in nearby Tus. From 1736 to 1796 it was the capital of Afsharid Iran, the dynasty founded by [[Nader Shah]], whose tomb is in the city.

Mosque in [[Mecca]], [[Saudi Arabia]], and the holiest mosque in [[Islam]]. It encloses the [[Kaaba]], the structure toward which Muslims pray, and it is the main site for the [[Hajj]] and ʿUmrah pilgrimages, whose rites include circumambulating the Kaaba. Islamic tradition holds that [[Abraham]] built the Kaaba, and the mosque is considered among the earliest in Islam. The Great Mosque contains the Black Stone, the Zamzam Well and the hills of Safa and Marwa. It has been expanded many times and is under the control of the King of Saudi Arabia, who also holds the title Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques. It is the largest mosque in the world.

Object normally worn on the face for protection, disguise, performance or ritual. Masks have been used since antiquity in ceremonies, hunting, feasts and war, as well as in [[Performing arts|performing arts]] and entertainment. They are sometimes used in drama therapy and psychotherapy. The Greek cult of [[Dionysus]] used masks in rites that temporarily suspended ordinary social roles. The [[Carnival]] of Venice, in which all are equal behind their masks, dates back to 1268. In art history, a mask is a face without a body, usually in low relief rather than modeled in the round. The English word appeared in the 1530s, from Middle French *masque*.
